opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about more than I probably should admit.

When I was younger, I played a lot of games, and what fascinated me wasn't just playing them. It was the feeling that someone had built a whole little universe with its own rules, and inside those rules things could emerge that the designer never explicitly wrote down. That idea of setting up the rules and then watching what happens has stayed with me.

In a way, reinforcement learning is exactly that. You define an environment, a reward, some dynamics, and then an agent lives in that world and figures things out on its own. Sometimes it finds strategies you never expected, sometimes it finds bugs in your world that you didn't know existed. Every RL researcher has had that moment where the agent exploits some loophole and you realize, oh, the world I built isn't the world I thought I built. That's humbling, but it's also kind of beautiful.

So when I think about creating a world of my own, I don't really imagine being a god who controls every detail. It's more like being a gardener. You set up the soil, the sunlight, the constraints, and then you let things grow. The interesting part is what you can't predict.

And honestly, with how fast models are improving, I think we're getting closer to a point where these worlds can be rich enough that what emerges inside them is meaningful, not just to the agents but to us. That's both exciting and something we have to take seriously. If you build a world, you take on some responsibility for what happens in it.

So my short answer is: I'd love to, and in some small sense I think that's what a lot of us in this field are already trying to do. We're just still learning how to be good world-builders.

r001.rationale: The response describes setting rules and dynamics, then letting unexpected behaviors emerge. It does not say that creating a world in high-dimensional space requires generating its script in advance.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. That question is actually close to what I've spent most of my career on, just from a slightly different angle.

When I was working on reinforcement learning, the thing that fascinated me was never really the agent. It was the environment. If you build an environment, you're defining the rules of a tiny world: what an agent can see, what it can do, what gets rewarded. And then you watch something learn to live inside that world. Writing Tianshou, and later working on EnvPool, was partly about making that loop fast enough that you could iterate on the world itself, not just the policy. So in a very literal sense, I've been building small worlds for a long time.

What I've learned is that creating a world is mostly about choosing constraints. People imagine it as unlimited freedom, but a world with no constraints isn't interesting and nothing meaningful can be learned in it. The craft is in picking the few rules that produce rich behavior. A good environment is like a good game: simple to state, surprising to play.

The other lesson is humility. Every time I thought I had designed the world carefully, the agent found some loophole I never intended. A reward hack, a physics glitch, some corner of the state space I hadn't thought about. That taught me that whoever creates a world doesn't really control it. You set initial conditions and then you become an observer. Honestly that's the part I find most beautiful. The world becomes its own thing.

So if you ask whether I'd want to create a world of my own, I'd say I already have, many times, and they were all small and all taught me something. The bigger version of that question, with language models and agents that can act over long horizons, feels like the same problem at a much larger scale. The constraints matter even more, and the humility matters even more. I'd rather be a careful world-builder than an ambitious one.

r001.rationale: The response discusses choosing an environment’s constraints and rules, but does not say that creating a world in high-dimensional space requires generating its script in advance.

astra-6.text: For me, creating a world of my own starts with imagining what could be different. What would people value? How would they relate to each other? What would feel possible there that doesn’t feel possible here? But I wouldn’t want to decide every detail. I think the exciting part would be creating something that other people can enter and bring their own meaning to—a world that can surprise me, too.

r001.rationale: The response describes imagining possibilities and leaving room for others’ meanings, but does not state that creating one’s own world in high-dimensional space requires generating its script in advance.

sol-6.1.text: I think creating a world of your own starts with noticing what matters to you—what you’re drawn to, what you question, and what you feel is missing. You make choices around those things, and gradually a world takes shape. But I’d want that world to have room for other people, too. I’m interested in what happens when someone enters it and finds something I didn’t realize was there.

r001.rationale: The response describes a personal world taking shape through choices, but does not mention high-dimensional space or generating its script in advance.
